accepted.label: Consider Many Different Viewpoints in Decision-Making
accepted.description: Great decisions are shaped by consideration of many different viewpoints, without seeking consensus but not acting unilaterally; it requires discernment on whose opinion to seek and when to force a solution.
coverage_criteria: Explain why considering many different viewpoints shapes great decisions.
Describe how to balance seeking input versus making a unilateral decision.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Make Decisions Close to the Action
accepted.description: Great decisions are made as close as possible to the action, involving those who do the work rather than only those in power, which requires trust and putting ego aside.
coverage_criteria: Describe why involving front-line workers improves decision quality.
Identify situations where it is better to seek advice from those at the operational level.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Address Root Cause in Decision-Making
accepted.description: Great decisions address the root cause of problems, not just symptoms, by engaging people who understand where issues originated and developing plans to fix the underlying cause.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate between symptoms and root causes in a decision context.
Explain why focusing on root causes leads to more effective decisions.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Assign Clear Accountability in Decisions
accepted.description: Great decisions are made by a clearly accountable person who stands behind their decisions, even if they later turn out to be mistakes.
coverage_criteria: Explain the importance of clear accountability in decision-making.
Describe how accountability fosters ownership and integrity in the decision process.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Balance Short-Term and Long-Term Value in Decisions
accepted.description: Great decisions consider the holistic impacts of a problem and balance long-term and short-term value, sometimes requiring sacrifice of immediate efficiency for long-term competence.
coverage_criteria: Discuss how to evaluate trade-offs between short-term gains and long-term value in decision-making.
Provide examples where short-term sacrifices lead to long-term benefits.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Communicate Decisions Effectively to Stakeholders
accepted.description: Great decisions are communicated well to stakeholders, involving honesty and integrity even when facing difficult audiences or consequences.
coverage_criteria: Outline key principles for effectively communicating decisions to stakeholders.
Explain the importance of transparency and integrity in decision communication.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Make Timely Decisions
accepted.description: Great decisions are timely; they avoid procrastination, fear of mistakes, or blame-shifting by charting the best course forward with available information and acting promptly.
coverage_criteria: Explain the importance of timeliness in decision-making.
Identify common barriers to timely decisions such as perfectionism or fear of disapproval.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Balance Gut Instinct with Team Considerations
accepted.description: While trusting one's gut can be valuable, great decisions also require considering whether that instinct is the best course for everyone involved.
coverage_criteria: Discuss the role of intuition in decision-making.
Describe when it is appropriate to rely on gut instinct versus when broader team or organizational considerations should prevail.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone principle from the source article on great decision-making.

accepted.label: Linear Thinking and Exponential Change
accepted.description: The cognitive limitation that humans think linearly, making it difficult to properly assess exponential technological growth, which can lead to flawed decisions about technology adoption.
coverage_criteria: Explain why humans are ill-suited to grasp exponential change.
Identify possible social consequences of rapid technological development.
Compare ex-ante and ex-post views on technological adoption.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone candidate on a cognitive bias impacting decision-making.

accepted.label: Outcome Bias and Evaluating Decision Quality
accepted.description: Outcome bias is the tendency to evaluate the quality of a decision based solely on its outcomes. To evaluate decisions effectively, one must consider the decision process and not just outcomes.
coverage_criteria: Define outcome bias and give an example.
Explain why evaluating decisions by outcomes alone can be misleading.
Describe how a process-based evaluation differs from an outcome-based evaluation.
accepted.merge_rationale: These two metadata candidates are closely related: one defines outcome bias, the other discusses the broader need to evaluate decisions beyond outcomes. Together they form a cohesive concept on avoiding outcome-based judgment.
